author: A Robot
objectives: Students will describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode, including the eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Students will explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Students will contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
Students will predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and that planet.
Students will compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: Observe the apparent retrograde motion of Mars from the perspective of Earth.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during a retrograde episode, including the eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
instructions: Observe the general eastward motion of Mars.
Notice Mars slowing down and reversing direction.
Watch as Mars completes its westward loop.
See Mars resume its eastward motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to the apparent retrograde motion of Mars as viewed from Earth.
clips.narration: Welcome! We'll begin by observing the night sky from Earth. Notice how planets like Mars generally move eastward against the background stars. But something peculiar happens periodically.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars begins its apparent westward loop.
clips.narration: Over time, Mars appears to slow down, stop its eastward motion, and begin to move westward. This is the beginning of its retrograde loop.
Mars continues its westward journey for a couple of months, creating a noticeable loop against the backdrop of stars. This puzzling behavior puzzled astronomers for centuries.
Finally, Mars appears to stop its westward motion and once again resumes its normal eastward drift. This complete cycle of apparent motion is what we call retrograde motion.

modules.description: Understand retrograde motion from an outside perspective in the heliocentric model.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Students will compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.
instructions: Observe the Sun, Earth, and outer planets in their orbits.
Note Earth's faster orbital speed compared to outer planets.
See how Earth overtaking Mars creates the illusion of retrograde motion.
Compare the apparent loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to the heliocentric model and relative orbital speeds.
clips.narration: Now, let's shift our perspective outside the solar system. Here, we see the Sun at the center, with Earth and the outer planets in their smooth, nearly circular orbits. Notice that Earth, being closer to the Sun, orbits faster than Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth overtakes Mars, causing apparent retrograde motion.
clips.narration: When Earth, moving faster, overtakes Mars in its orbit, Mars appears to slow down, stop, and move backward relative to the background stars. This is precisely why retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model. It's an illusion caused by relative motion, much like when a faster car overtakes a slower one on the highway.

clips.changeMeaning: Comparing retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
clips.narration: Let's now consider Jupiter and Saturn. Because they are farther from the Sun, they move much slower in their orbits. This means Earth overtakes them less frequently, and the apparent retrograde loops they produce are smaller and less dramatic than Mars's. The more distant the planet, the smaller its retrograde loop.
